title: At the café
goal: Order food and drinks — while facing the Akkusativ, a change in the article that sounds scary but touches only one box out of four.
bekal: turn a masculine article into the Akkusativ (*einen Kaffee*)
ask for the bill and pay

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bestellen und bezahlen
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at a small café in Kreuzberg. Budi and Lena sit outside. Watch the form of the article every time something is ordered.

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.text: Guten Tag. Was möchten Sie trinken?
lines.id: Hello. What would you like to drink?
lines.literal: good day. what would-like you drink?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Mit Milch.
lines.id: I'd like a coffee, please. With milk.
lines.literal: I would-like a coffee, please. with milk.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Und ich nehme einen Tee und ein Wasser.
lines.id: And I'll have a tea and a water.
lines.literal: and I take a tea and a water.

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.id: Would you like something to eat too?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: Yes, I'll have an apple cake.

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.text: Tut mir leid, wir haben keine Sandwiches mehr. Aber wir haben eine Suppe.
lines.id: Sorry, we're out of sandwiches. But we have a soup.
lines.literal: does to-me sorrow, we have no sandwiches more. but we have a soup.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Gut, dann nehme ich die Suppe.
lines.id: OK, then I'll have the soup.
lines.literal: good, then take I the soup.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: Excuse me, we'd like to pay, please.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Zusammen, bitte. Wie viel macht das?
lines.id: Together, please. How much is that?
lines.literal: together, please. how much makes that?

notes: **Lines 2 and 3: *einen*, not *ein*.** As soon as a thing becomes the **object** of an action — what's ordered, bought, drunk, seen — its masculine article changes: *ein → einen*, *der → den*. Feminine and neuter words don't change at all. That's the whole of the Akkusativ.

***Ich möchte* and *Ich nehme* are both polite.** *Möchte* ("I'd like") sounds soft; *nehme* ("I'll take") is quicker and just as common. What you **don't** use is *Ich will* ("I want") — it sounds like a child making demands.
**The most polite form: *Ich hätte gern…*** ("I would gladly have"). It's a conditional form only taken apart at A2, but as a fixed phrase it's very useful now: *Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee, bitte.*

***Tut mir leid*** literally means "does me sorrow" = "I'm sorry". Keep it apart from *Entschuldigung*, which is used to get someone's attention or apologize for a small disturbance — like English *excuse me*.
***keine … mehr*** = "no more …", for things that have run out. The pattern: *kein* before the noun, *mehr* at the end. *Wir haben keinen Kaffee mehr.*
**Line 8: *dann nehme ich…*** The sentence starts with *dann*, so the subject steps behind the verb. The same rule as *Jetzt wohne ich…* in Unit 2, taken apart fully in Unit 10.

grammars.title: Akkusativ: the one box that changes
body: German marks a noun's role in the sentence through its article. The subject takes the **Nominativ** form; the object of the action takes the **Akkusativ** form. The good news was already mentioned above — only masculine words really change. (English does this only with pronouns: *he* → *him*.)
after: Compare these two sentences: ***Der** Kaffee ist gut* (coffee = subject, Nominativ) and *Ich trinke **den** Kaffee* (coffee = what's drunk, Akkusativ). Same word, different role, different form.
Possessives follow the same rule because they follow *ein*: *mein → meinen*, *dein → deinen*, *sein → seinen*, *unser → unseren*. *Ich sehe **meinen** Bruder* but *Ich sehe **meine** Schwester*.

The verbs that call for the Akkusativ are verbs that have an object: *haben, nehmen, kaufen, trinken, essen, sehen, lesen, brauchen, möchten, suchen, finden*. On the other hand, ***sein*** never takes the Akkusativ — whatever follows *sein* stays Nominativ: *Das ist **ein** Kaffee*.

grammars.title: möchten — the ordering verb
body: *Möchten* is really a conditional form of *mögen* (to like), but it's used so often as a word of its own that it's better to learn it as a complete verb now.
after: ⚠️ Notice that *ich* and *er/sie/es* use **exactly the same** form, with no *-t* ending for *er*. This is typical of the whole group of helper verbs you'll meet again in Unit 11 (*kann*, *muss*, *will*).

If *möchten* is followed by another verb, that verb is sent to the **end of the sentence** in its basic form: *Ich möchte einen Kaffee **trinken***. This bracket structure is one of the most distinctive features of German, and all of Unit 11 is devoted to it.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Water in Germany is almost always sparkling unless you ask otherwise. Plain *ein Wasser* will arrive fizzy; if you want still water, ask for ***ein stilles Wasser***. And free tap water isn't the custom — ordering *Leitungswasser* is fine, but don't be surprised if it's on the bill.

head: German
English
rows: What would you like to drink?

blocks.text: The last question matters more than it seems: many small cafés in Germany **only take cash**, and a sign saying *Nur Barzahlung* on the door means exactly that. Always carry some bills.
The quickest way to tell them apart: ask *wer?* (who is doing it) for the Nominativ, and *wen?* or *was?* (whom/what is it done to) for the Akkusativ — just like English *who* and *whom*.

blocks.title: If you only have time to learn one thing from this unit
items: Learn this: **der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen, mein → meinen**. They all add -en, and only for masculine words.
Feminine, neuter and plural words don't change at all in the Akkusativ. Three quarters of the table is a copy.
After *sein* there's never an Akkusativ: *Das ist ein Kaffee*, not *das ist einen Kaffee*.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct Akkusativ form: *einen*, *eine* or *ein*.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: What would you like to drink? — I'd like a coffee, please. — We're out of sandwiches. — Then I'll have the soup. — The bill, please. — Together or separately?
einen — eine — ein — einen — einen — ein
Ich möchte einen Kaffee. — Wir möchten die Rechnung. — Was möchten Sie trinken? — Ich trinke keinen Wein. — Dann nehme ich die Suppe. — Zusammen oder getrennt?
